Research

Two questions.
One physical world.

Can a model trained on simulations work with real measurements? And when sensors are limited, where should we place them? My MPhil thesis investigates both questions in water distribution networks.

01 Transfer learning · Interpretability

Across the
reality gap.

Simulations can generate many labeled examples of pressure transients. Experimental leak records are much harder to obtain. I pre-trained models on simulated signals, adapted them using limited experimental data, and used Integrated Gradients to examine which sensor–time regions shaped their predictions.

The study found that later, multiply scattered wave information can be useful for diagnosis—an insight that only matters if it remains visible when the model meets real data.

02 Sensor optimization

Where should
we listen?

Installing sensors everywhere is rarely practical. My Deep Contrastive Sensor Selection framework learns a subset of measurement locations for the diagnostic task, combining supervised contrastive learning with differentiable Top‑K selection.

In the Q‑Leak case study, the method is compared with a mutual-information-motivated baseline across sensor budgets and noise levels. The baseline remains stronger in some extremely noisy, low-budget settings; that limitation is part of the result.
